misfits.thing: Asphalt road with white dashed and solid lane markings

misfits.thing: Paved asphalt road with white dashed lane markings
misfits.where: Center and right of the image, running through the village street

misfits.thing: Curb stones along the road edge

misfits.thing: Paved asphalt road with white dashed lane markings

misfits.thing: Brick chimney on the thatched cottage
misfits.where: Top left, rising from the roof of the nearest house
misfits.why: Its neat rectangular masonry stack looks more like a later-period brick chimney than the rough medieval stone or wattle fittings typical of c. 1350 village houses.

misfits.thing: White hen with red comb among the chickens
misfits.where: Lower left foreground, near the fence
misfits.why: Chickens of this breed and uniform plumage look like modern domestic breeds rather than medieval fowl, which were typically smaller and more varied in color.

misfits.thing: White church tower with red pointed roof and cross on top

misfits.thing: Brick chimney on the right-hand cottage
misfits.where: Top right, above the thatched roof of the cottage on the right edge
misfits.why: Its reddish, regularly coursed brick looks more like a later construction than the rubble or stone chimneys of a village around 1350.

misfits.thing: Hens with modern-looking plumage (reddish-brown and blue-speckled birds)
misfits.where: Lower left, pecking near the wooden fence
misfits.why: Their colouring and markings resemble standardized breeds developed in the 19th century, not the landrace fowl typical of a 14th-century village.

misfits.thing: Stone chimney with rising smoke on the thatched cottage at upper right
misfits.where: Top right, on the roof of the far-right cottage, against the sky
misfits.why: Freestanding chimneys on peasant houses were rare around 1350; such cottages usually vented smoke through a central hearth or the roof, and chimneys became common only later.

misfits.thing: Black metal street lamp with a glass globe
misfits.where: Right foreground, along the edge of the sidewalk beside the shop
misfits.why: Electric-style street lighting with a modern lamp housing does not exist in 1st-century Rome; Romans used oil lamps or torches, not fixtures like this.

misfits.thing: Tiled red roof edge with wooden window shutters and whitewashed walls
misfits.where: Upper left and center buildings
misfits.why: Largely plausible for Roman architecture, so not a misfit.

misfits.thing: Metal street lamp with glass lantern head
misfits.where: Right side of the image, along the building facade and sidewalk edge
misfits.why: Modern-style cast metal streetlight with an enclosed lamp; 1st-century Roman streets were lit by oil lamps or torches, not electric-style street lamps.

misfits.thing: Smooth white canvas awnings over the shop fronts
misfits.where: Above the shop doorways on the right and in the mid-background
misfits.why: Retractable fabric awnings over shopfronts are plausible but the clean, modern rigid frame styling of the awning brackets looks more like a later period shopfront design than Roman.

misfits.thing: Black iron street lamp with a glass-enclosed electric-style light bulb
misfits.where: Right side of the image, along the sidewalk edge near the building corner
misfits.why: Modern-style cast iron street lamp with a bulb fixture; Roman streets of the 1st century AD used oil lamps or torches, not this design.

misfits.thing: Wooden shop awning and shutters with modern-looking construction
misfits.where: Shopfront awning over the pottery shop and upper window shutters
misfits.why: The angled wooden awning brackets and paneled shutters resemble later medieval or modern design rather than typical Roman street architecture.

misfits.thing: Smooth, large rectangular stone paving slabs with a neat grid pattern
misfits.where: Foreground street surface
misfits.why: Roman streets used irregular polygonal stones or basalt blocks; the regular, finely cut slab grid looks more like a modern or late-medieval pavement.

misfits.thing: Modern metal street lamp with a glowing lamp head
misfits.where: Right side of the image, along the sidewalk edge beside the shop front
misfits.why: Street lighting of this form is a modern fixture; a 1st-century Roman street would have used oil lamps or torches, not an electric-style metal lamp post.

misfits.thing: Modern street lamp with a dark metal pole and enclosed electric-style light fixture
misfits.where: Right side of the street, next to the shop doorway and the amphora
misfits.why: Street lighting of this form is a modern invention; Roman streets of the 1st century AD had no such electric-style lamp post.

misfits.thing: Glowing wall lantern in the shop doorway and oil-lit lamp shapes
misfits.where: Upper left of the open shop doorway, near the hanging goods
misfits.why: The enclosed lantern is a more modern style; Romans used oil lamps, not this lantern form, though this is a minor point.

misfits.thing: Modern-style metal street lamp with a dome shade and electric-looking glowing bulb
misfits.where: Right side of the image, along the sidewalk edge next to the building
misfits.why: Street lighting like this is anachronistic for a 1st century AD Roman street; Romans did not have such fixtures, and this one resembles a modern lamppost.

misfits.thing: Metal awning or canvas awning supported by a metal bracket frame
misfits.where: Upper middle of the image above the shop entrance and the red awning further left
misfits.why: The retractable canvas awning hardware with metal brackets and rails looks like a modern shopfront design rather than an ancient Roman feature.

misfits.thing: Ornate scrolled wrought-iron wall bracket holding the hanging lamp
misfits.where: Upper left, on the wall above the shopfront awning
misfits.why: Its elaborate curling scrollwork resembles Renaissance or later ironwork more than the simpler fittings typical of 1st-century Roman buildings.

misfits.thing: Wall-mounted hanging oil lamp with ornate wrought-iron bracket and chain
misfits.where: Upper right of the shopfront, beside the doorway
misfits.why: Hanging oil lamps existed in Roman times, but this one has a decorative scrolled wrought-iron bracket that looks more like a later medieval or Victorian style fixture than a Roman lamp.

misfits.thing: Hanging wall lantern with glass panes and chain
misfits.where: Upper left, mounted on the wrought-iron bracket beside the shop doorway
misfits.why: Its enclosed glass-walled housing and chain suspension look more like a later medieval or modern lantern than the open bronze or terracotta oil lamps typical of 1st-century Roman streets.

misfits.thing: Glass window with multi-pane wooden sash frame
misfits.where: right wall, behind the woman
misfits.why: Small multi-pane glazed windows are anachronistic for a ca. 900 Viking longhouse, which would have had shuttered openings or no glass.

misfits.thing: Smoke hole skylight with glazed/framed opening
misfits.where: top left of the ceiling
misfits.why: The skylight appears to be a framed opening with glass-like panel, more consistent with later construction than a simple smoke hole in a ca. 900 longhouse.

misfits.thing: Wire-like metal tripod cooking stand with iron chain and hook
misfits.where: center left, over the fire pit
misfits.why: The sturdy wrought-iron tripod with a chain-hung cauldron is plausible, but its neat hardware and hinged arm look more like a later medieval design than an early Viking one.

misfits.thing: Multi-pane window with a wooden grid and clear glass-looking panes
misfits.where: Right side of the back wall, beside the seated family
misfits.why: Clear glass windows with a muntin grid were not used in a Viking Age longhouse around 900; openings were typically unglazed or covered with cloth, hide, or shutters.

misfits.thing: Window with a multi-pane grid of clear glass
misfits.where: Right side of the back wall, beside the woman with the spear
misfits.why: Window glass was not common in Scandinavian houses around 900; openings were typically unglazed shutters or smoke holes, so a paned glass window looks anachronistic.

misfits.thing: Multi-paned window with a white frame
misfits.where: Center-right of the back wall, between the two shields, above the seated family
misfits.why: Large framed window with a grid of small panes looks like glazed glass with a modern window frame, which would be unusual in a house around 900. Viking-age longhouses had small openings or shutters rather than framed glass windows.

misfits.thing: Glass window with multiple small rectangular panes and a wooden frame

misfits.why: Multi-paned glass windows were not used in Viking-age houses around 900; openings were typically unglazed or covered with cloth, hide, or shutters.

misfits.thing: Skylight opening in the roof showing sky
misfits.where: Top center of the ceiling above the hearth
misfits.why: A glazed or open roof skylight of this kind is anachronistic; Viking longhouses ventilated smoke through an open gap or roof vent without a framed skylight design like this.

misfits.thing: Multi-pane glazed window with a wooden grid
misfits.where: Center-right wall, between the bearded man and the shield
misfits.why: Around 900 AD Scandinavian longhouses had no glazed window panes. Light came through open smoke holes or small shuttered openings, so a framed, multi-pane window looks anachronistic.

misfits.thing: Rectangular skylight-style opening in the roof

misfits.why: A neatly framed rectangular opening in the roof resembles a modern skylight, which would be anachronistic for a Viking longhouse around 900 AD, where roofs had simple smoke vents or open gaps.

misfits.thing: Rectangular glazed skylight in the roof
